title: New every morning (Lamentations 3:22–23)
hook: in the ruins, the mercies of the Lord are not consumed

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant, the law moved from stone to the innermost part of a person. Your line was written on the heart. Where did you catch it showing through? Day four hundred twenty-four.

Here's a strange fact about grief: someone once wrote it out in alphabetical order. The Book of Lamentations is five poems about Jerusalem after the Babylonians burned it, around 587 before Christ. The walls are down, the Temple is ash, children are begging for bread in the streets. And four of the five poems are acrostics: each verse, or each set of verses, starts with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to tav. Maybe it was a way to hold sorrow that has no shape. A complete grief, A to Z. And right in the middle of the middle poem, something turns.
screen: `GRIEF IN ALPHABETICAL ORDER.` → `A CITY IN ASHES, 587 BC.` → `IN THE MIDDLE, SOMETHING TURNS.`

segments.voice: Chapter three is the longest poem, sixty-six verses, three for each letter. It begins with a man who says, in effect: I am the one who has seen affliction. He's been walled in, weighed down with chains, his prayers shut out, his teeth broken on gravel. He says his hope has perished. It's about as dark as the Bible gets. Then at verse twenty-one he says: this I call back to mind, and so I have hope. And then the lines the hook is named for, in the Douay-Rheims: "The mercies of the Lord that we are not consumed: because his commiserations have not failed. They are new every morning, great is thy faithfulness." Commiserations is an old word for compassion. In Hebrew it's rachamim, a word related to the word for womb: the love a mother has for the child she carried. Notice what the poet doesn't say. He doesn't say the city is fine. It isn't. The ruins are still there when he looks up. He says the mercies are not used up. Like manna in the desert, they don't keep overnight; they come new, each morning, enough for the day. Tradition gives the book to Jeremiah, though the poems themselves name no author. For centuries Catholics sang Lamentations in the dark services of Holy Week called Tenebrae, candles going out one by one. And Jews read it on Tisha B'Av, the day of mourning for the Temple. Both keep this book for the worst days, because it doesn't pretend. It just finds, in the middle of the alphabet, one thing that hasn't run out.
screen: `I AM THE ONE WHO HAS SEEN AFFLICTION.` · `THIS I CALL TO MIND.` · `RACHAMIM: A MOTHER'S COMPASSION.` · `THE RUINS ARE STILL THERE.` · then, large: `THEY ARE NEW EVERY MORNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan tomorrow's first thank you. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last day. Not the whole thing, just look for one mercy that came anyway, in the middle of whatever else was going on. A text from someone. Hot water. A person who was kind on a bad day. Hold it for a moment. Now picture tomorrow morning, the minute you wake, before you reach for your phone. Decide now what you'll do then: say thank you, for one thing, first. If you pray, it can be to God, with this line from Lamentations. The bell holds the time.
New every morning. The poet's line in the ruins of Jerusalem: the Lord's mercies aren't used up, they come fresh each day. Today's word.
Your line: his mercies are new. Tomorrow, first thing, before the phone, thank God, or just say thank you, for one thing. Day four hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: For centuries Catholics sang passages of Lamentations at Tenebrae during Holy Week, and many Catholics begin the day with a morning offering or Morning Prayer, thanking God before anything else.

fork.setup: you're the poet. your city is ash and your hope, you say, has perished. what do you write next?
options: that everything is fine after all.
that the mercies of the Lord are not used up; they're new every morning.
fork.reveal: "they are new every morning, great is thy faithfulness." the ruins don't go away; the mercies come anyway.

original.note: Hebrew: new (plural), from Lamentations 3:23, new every morning.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cheerful verse for a coffee mug.
what it means: a line written in the ashes of Jerusalem, at the center of a poem of grief, by someone who still saw the ruins.
what a scholar hears: it sits in the third of five acrostic poems, three verses per letter; rachamim, compassion, shares its root with rechem, womb.
